name: sla-misses-detector
context: A data pipeline's promise is not 'the process is up' but 'data is fresh, complete and correct within X'. This pattern evaluates pipeline service-level indicators against their objectives over rolling windows and emits structured, severity-classified alerts when the objective is being missed — a page for an error budget burning fast, a ticket for slow erosion. Freshness is measured as the age of the oldest unprocessed item or the most recently processed item; correctness as a ratio of processing errors to items processed; completeness as the fraction of expected volume observed.
benefits: Converts an unbounded stream of raw metrics into a small number of alerts that correspond to user-visible loss
Severity falls out of the burn rate, so paging is reserved for events that will exhaust the error budget, not for every threshold crossing
Multiwindow checks (page when the long window and a 1/12-length short window both breach) cut false positives without losing detection speed
Makes the error budget an explicit, spendable quantity that teams can trade against release velocity
Windowed SLIs catch chronic sub-threshold degradation that instantaneous checks miss
tradeoffs: Burn-rate alerting needs a minimum event rate; a pipeline processing a handful of records an hour cannot be distinguished from one failing
Objective selection is a business decision, and a wrong objective produces confident, worthless alerts
Multiwindow rules are more complex to author and to explain at 3am than a single threshold
Very high availability objectives cannot be defended by alerting — a 100% outage can exhaust a 99.999% budget faster than the alert pipeline can deliver a page
Alerts that classify hard misses without suppressing known-benign windows degrade into noise and get muted
use_cases: Freshness SLO: 99% of records reach the serving table within 100 seconds, measured as a distribution cut over pipeline lag
Completeness SLO: the hourly ingest volume is at least 99.5% of the previous hour's volume
Correctness SLO: fewer than 0.5% of items in a calendar month contain schema or range errors
Windowed freshness: 99% of five-minute windows over a rolling day never exceeded the lag threshold
Classifying an SLA miss as a hard miss requiring paging versus a soft miss that opens a ticket
avoid_when: No objective has been agreed with the business — the pattern needs a target, not just a metric
The signal is a low-rate, bursty event stream where burn rate is statistically meaningless
Only infrastructure health is available (CPU, disk) and no pipeline-level SLI can be derived
The consumer of the alert is automated remediation with no human in the loop — that is a policy engine, not an SLO
component_types: SLI definitions: correctness ratio, freshness distribution cut, completeness ratio, each expressed over a rolling window
Objective store: the target percentage, rolling period and error budget derived from it
Burn-rate evaluator: ratio of observed bad-event rate to the SLO's allowed error rate
Multiwindow gate: a long window plus a short window (roughly 1/12 its length) that must both breach before firing
Severity classifier: page versus ticket, derived from the fraction of budget consumed
Emission channel: structured alert with the objective, window, observed value and budget remaining
anti_patterns: Alerting on a raw lag threshold, which fires constantly on bursty pipelines and stays silent on slowly degrading ones
Using only infrastructure metrics (CPU, memory) as a proxy for pipeline health
Treating SLO compliance as binary, hiding the difference between a 1% and a 60% budget burn
Paging on a single slow window with no burn-rate gating
Alerting on percentiles of a signal whose population changes at night, so the very p99 that mattered yesterday is now routine
design_principles: Alert on user-visible loss, not on component state
Budget, not threshold: the unit of concern is how fast the error budget is being spent
Multiwindow confirmation: fast detection with slow reset, so the alert neither misses nor cries wolf
Severity derived from burn rate, never from the metric that tripped
Every alert carries enough context to act without opening the dashboard
best_practices: Start the rolling period at 28 days — long enough for strategic and tactical use, short enough to react to
Express SLIs as good-events over total-events so the objective maps directly onto an error budget
Implement multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerts rather than a single threshold; page on 14.4x over 1h confirmed by 5m, ticket on 6x over 6h
For streaming pipelines use lag age, not lag count — records and seconds are different units
Alert on windowed SLIs as well as request-based ones so chronic slowness is visible
